https://aa.com.tr/en/world/nato-holds-ai.text: World Eurasia NATO holds air exercise near Russia's Kaliningrad region Planned operation unrelated to Russian air-force activity, say Polish commanders Şeyma Erkul Dayanç 20 August 2026 • Update : 20 August 2026 İSTANBUL NATO conducted a planned air exercise above northeastern Poland near Russia's Kaliningrad region Tuesday, according to Polish broadcaster TVP World. The exercise involved US and Norwegian fighter jets, a NATO E-3A Sentry AWACS surveillance aircraft, aerial-refueling tankers and a US EA-37B electronic-warfare aircraft. Estimates of the number of aircraft involved ranged from about 25 to 50. Poland's Operational Command said the exercise was coordinated by NATO and was unrelated to Russian air force activity. The operation was intended to strengthen interoperability among allied forces and practice joint air-operation scenarios, according to the command. The exercise came days after the Bild newspaper in Germany reported details of what it described as a NATO Land Warfighting Concept for responding to a possible Russian attack on the Baltic states. The reported concept includes potential strikes against missile and air-defense systems in the Kaliningrad region. NATO has increased military exercises around the strategically important Suwalki Gap, a narrow stretch of territory connecting Poland and Lithuania between Kaliningrad and Belarus. https://nineoclock.ro/alexandru-petrescu.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Alexandru Petrescu , President of the Financial Supervisory Authority: The Future of European Capital Markets and the Savings and Investments Union Delighted to attend as a keynote speaker at the Hellenic Capital Market Commission Symposium 2026 in Athens on September 9, an important forum bringing together regulators, policymakers and market leaders to discuss the future of European capital markets. I will contribute to the session dedicated to the Future of European Capital Markets and the Savings and Investments Union, a project that can become one of the key instruments for strengthening Europe’s competitiveness and its capacity to finance sustainable economic growth. From Romania’s perspective, this debate comes at a particularly relevant moment. Our capital market has gained significant momentum, while the next stage of development requires deeper liquidity, broader retail participation, stronger access to capital for companies and a more effective connection between domestic savings and productive investment. The Savings and Investments Union can accelerate this process, provided that European integration works in practice for markets of every size and that common rules translate into tangible opportunities for issuers and investors across all Member States. European scale should strengthen local markets, while investor protection, proportionality and confidence must remain at the heart of this transformation. I look forward to the discussions in Athens and to exchanging views with fellow regulators and market leaders on how we can build deeper, more competitive and more accessible European capital markets, capable of supporting innovation, investment and long-term prosperity. https://www.eurasiareview.com/12092026-w.text: The Northern Dvina river in Russia. Photo Credit: Ipaat, Wikipedia Commons Analysis 1 Environment Europe September 12, 2026 September 12, 2026 Paul Goble 0 Comments By Paul Goble Key Takeaways: The author argues Russia is facing spreading water shortages from climate change and heavier use—not only its famous spring floods. Effects cited include weaker harvests, Europe’s largest desert growing in the south (~500 km² a year), and drinking-water strain in cities and villages. Falling rivers, the Caspian, and Arctic ports, the piece says, hurt domestic shipping and bulk exports, undercut talk of selling or diverting Siberian water to Central Asia or China, silt the North–South/Iran route, and limit the Northern Sea Route for deep-draft ships. Moscow is described as taking only small steps (dredging, foreign help on rivers) so as not to divert money from the Ukraine war. Ukraine’s recent strikes on water networks are presented as turning a long-term problem into an immediate political risk. These are the author’s conclusions from Russian and other reporting. Better known for its massive spring flooding than for its occasional droughts, Russia is now being hit across the board by water shortages in ever more parts of the country. Accelerating climate change and growing human use are leading to declines in food production for domestic use and export, desertification—Russia now has the largest desert in Europe— and restrictions on riverine and coastal shipping, including the critical Northern Sea Route (NSR) and North–South Route via the Caspian Sea ( Fond Strategicheskoi Kul’tury , February 8; Gorizontal’naya Rossiya , August 5; Stolitie , August 11; The Moscow Times , August 26). This trend has limited Moscow’s ability to use water as a political weapon in neighboring regions such as Central Asia—likely killing any chance of Siberian river diversion to that region, which might help hold it in the Russian orbit—and to earn money by selling it to the People’s Republic of China (PRC), which has its own water shortage problems. These issues also compromise the possibility that Russia will be a major “water power” in the future ( Plotina.Net! , May 11, 2019; Noviye Izvestiya , June 3, 2023; VFokuse , April 7). Despite warning signs, Moscow, while clearly concerned, has yet to take the kind of concerted action that might make a big difference, limiting itself to small steps, such as inviting other countries to help deepen its rivers and expanding domestic dredging capacity, lest it take more significant ones that would take money away from Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war against Ukraine (see EDM , February 24, 2023; Window on Eurasia , August 9). That stance is becoming politically unsustainable given that Ukraine is now targeting Russia’s water distribution networks ( The Moscow Times , August 12). Every spring, Russia suffers from massive flooding as snow and ice melt and rivers overflow their banks. This unwelcome surfeit of water, however, also serves as a reminder of how much freshwater Russia possesses and thus has distracted attention from the far greater problems increasing shortages of water—brought about by climate change and expanded human use—are producing ( Gorizontal’naya Rossiya , August 5; URA.RU , September 5). Ignoring this has become impossible. Perhaps most immediately dramatic for the Russian population are new potable water shortages in major cities and the emergence of what is now the largest desert in Europe in the southern part of the country. This dead zone is currently expanding by more than 500 square kilometers (193 square miles) a year, reducing food crops in neighboring areas and sending prices skyrocketing (Window on Eurasia, November 17, 2024 , August 11 ). Russians are growing furious about both developments at a time when they are fed stories about flooding and the possibility that Russia will use water as a major foreign policy tool ( Kedr.Media , August 12, 2025). Their anger has been compounded by shortages of potable water in Russian villages and even major cities, a problem that also reflects a broader collapse in civic infrastructure ( Govorit NeMoskva , August 5; Nakanune.ru, August 21; Yesli Byt’ Tochnym , September 5). Moscow officials appear less concerned about that than about three other larger and longer-term problems and one immediate one. First, they worry about the impact of falling water levels on Russia’s rivers, a development that is compromising the country’s transportation system both domestically and internationally. Domestically, the riverine system has collapsed not only because Moscow has failed to build new vessels but also because falling water levels mean that older and larger vessels can no longer ply rivers that are not being dredged sufficiently to keep them open and support both the economies of Russia’s far-flung regions and its export capabilities. Because domestic shipping plays an outsize role in supporting Russian exports of bulk cargo such as coal, grain, and oil, this is also affecting Russia’s ability to earn money internationally ( Sibirskiy Ekonomist , January 18; Nezavisimaya Gazeta , July 2). Second, Moscow officials also appear disturbed that Russia’s own water shortages will prevent it from the possibility of sending water to Central Asia, as it has suggested it might do, and to the PRC. Russia very much wants to keep Central Asia in its zone of influence and to both earn money and cement its alliance with Beijing. Falling water levels inside Russia have likely killed off talk about the diversion of Siberian river water southward. They are also limiting the possibility of sales to the PRC even though many in Moscow very much want to carry through with its plans ( Plotina.Net! , May 11, 2019; VFokuse , April 7). Third, Moscow appears particularly alarmed that falling water levels on the Caspian and the silting up of both ports and at-sea portions of the NSR are already limiting Russia’s export capacities. These issues are even triggering conflicts with neighbors and allies Moscow hoped to keep sweet. The silting up of the Caspian has advanced so far that Moscow’s ability to use it as a north–south corridor to Iran has been constrained. Currently, only smaller ships or more lightly loaded larger ones can now make this passage (see EDM , March 18, 2025; Fond Strategicheskoi Kul’tury , February 8). As this has happened, tensions have increased between Russia and its neighbors who are demanding a say in how the Russian government manages the flow of the Volga, which feeds the waters of the Caspian (see EDM , June 3, 2025; Versia , August 4, 2025). The declining water level of the Caspian is also reducing the relative power of the Russian Navy’s Caspian Flotilla compared with the navies of other littoral countries, which have smaller but more numerous ships (see EDM, June 24, 2021 , January 27 ). At the same time, the situation on the NSR is, if anything, even more a matter of concern. Few of the ports along it are deep enough to handle larger container ships. Now, given the influx of sediment from the mainland as a result of the accelerated melting of permafrost, there are some places on the sea lane of the NSR itself not deep enough for such ships, which are larger, heavier, and with deeper drafts than most cargo vessels, to pass safely ( The Moscow Times , August 26). Until Moscow can build more dredging vessels or until it decides to seek to have the PRC play an even larger role in the Arctic than it has up to now, such bottlenecks are going to put a crimp on plans to ramp up the volume of shipping of finished goods as opposed to bulk cargo in the Arctic. These three long-term problems have now been eclipsed and exacerbated by a more immediate one that Moscow cannot ignore. Ukraine has now recognized Russia’s water shortage problems as a serious chokepoint and, a month ago, began targeting Russia’s water supply networks. This move could turn Russia’s water problems into a major political crisis in Moscow ( The Moscow Times , August 12). https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/opp.text: The Budapest Times Opposition accuses Tisza of sneaking ‘gender law’ past voters The parliamentary group leader of the Christian Democratic People's Party is accusing the government of planning to pass legislation next week, aimed at strengthening children's rights and safety, that is in fact a "gender law" running counter to the results of the 2022 referendum. In a video posted on his Facebook page on Thursday, Bence Rétvári said the legislation represents a return to the pre-2010 situation, with the Tisza government implementing a European Court ruling on gender matters in exchange for EU funds. “Organisations promoting gender reassignment or LGBT issues will once again be allowed into schools to give presentations, and such classes can be held in schools without the knowledge of parents. Gender can be freely promoted in the media and in books that minors can also access,” said the KDNP parliamentary group leader. He said the obligation to classify LGBT content as suitable only for those aged 18 and over would be abolished, and that nothing would then stand in the way of “Csipkejózsika books in schools.” He said Tisza Párt is going against the results of the 2022 referendum, in which people made it clear they did not want gender ideology in schools. He assessed that Tisza Párt places greater importance on Brussels’ expectations than on Hungarian families or the unambiguous result of the Hungarian referendum. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Politicians of all stripes appear eager to associate their opponents with the late sex offender. Photograph: Reuters View image in fullscreen Politicians of all stripes appear eager to associate their opponents with the late sex offender. Photograph: Reuters US midterm elections 2026 Ads accusing Republican candidates of protecting Epstein fill airwaves in final midterm push But select Democrats, too, are being accused of having ties to the late sex offender as country prepares to vote Ariana Baio Sat 31 Oct 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 11.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google In races across the country, Democratic candidates or groups that support them have released ads accusing Republicans of protecting pedophiles by voting against legislation to release files related to Jeffrey Epstein . The ads appear intended to evoke an emotional response by accusing candidates of “protecting” Epstein, a notorious pedophile accused of running a sex-trafficking ring involving minors. An analysis from CNN found that candidates and outside groups have spent more than $35m on Epstein-related ads. Another from the Washington Post found that Democrats spent more than $40m on Epstein-related ads across six key Senate races. The Epstein files are a sledgehammer for the US midterms | Katie Phang Read more In Colorado, ads targeting Republican Jeff Crank note that the lawmaker voted against releasing the Epstein files. In one , the family members of Virginia Giuffre, a woman who survived abuse at the hands of Epstein and died by suicide last year, claim Crank “covered up Epstein’s crimes to protect Donald Trump”. Ashley Hinson, a Senate candidate in Iowa, was accused of voting to “protect her donors” by refusing to vote to release the Epstein files. “This week I had to explain to my boys, ‘No, Mom does not protect pedophiles,’” Hinson said in a campaign ad responding to attacks over the Epstein files. An ad targeting Mike Collins , the Republican running for a Georgia Senate seat, says “Mike Collins voted against releasing the Epstein files even after he knew Epstein’s sex-trafficking operation exploited 14-year-old girls for sex”. Florida Republican Jimmy Patronis faced an attack from his Democratic opponent, claiming he called investigating Epstein “a waste of his time”. A spokesperson for Crank’s campaign accused the Epstein-related ad of being “intentionally vague”, in a statement to the Washington Post, because his position was that he would vote against the file’s release until he could be confident that victim information was properly redacted. The campaign also said it was “unfortunate” that his opponent, Jessica Killin, was “preying on a grieving family with the help of the Washington Democrats”. Crank’s staff invited and met with Giuffre’s family, though Crank himself did not meet with them in person, the New York Times reported. Crank’s campaign also said it offered to meet with Epstein victims before the vote on the legislation. Last year, Democrats and a select few House Republicans tried to force a vote on the Epstein files through a discharge petition – a procedure used in Congress to bypass the traditional steps of legislation and force a vote on the House floor. Donald Trump, who knew Epstein in the 1990s and early 2000s, opposed the discharge petition for the files, reversing his campaign promise to increase government transparency. House Republicans largely aligned themselves with him, prompting anger from high-profile Trump voters. Eventually, under pressure from allies, Trump supported the legislation, giving Republican lawmakers the go-ahead to vote for it. All but one House Republican voted for the Epstein Files Transparency Act. Many of the ads omit the fact that nearly every House Republican voted to release the Epstein files when the Epstein Files Transparency Act came to the floor, although at that point Trump had agreed to sign the legislation and release the files. Instead, the ads refer to Republicans opposing early attempts to force the legislation to the floor. Republicans have pointed to this fact when disputing the attack ads. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “Of course I voted to release the Epstein files,” Hinson said in a direct-to-camera ad, accusing her opponent, Josh Turek, of lying. While Hinson voted for the final Epstein Files Transparency Act, she did not sign on to the discharge petition. Patronis, meanwhile, never called the investigation a “waste of time”, but told a local radio station that while he had “no problem getting everything all released”, the issue was a “massive energy and time suck at the end of the day”. Melissa Stone, a spokesperson for Patronis’s campaign, highlighted his work with Trump to obtain disaster funding after Hurricane Isaias and said his opponent, Gay Valimont, was “still talking about a dead pedophile in a sad web video than helping the people of [the first congressional district] recover.” Some Republicans and groups supporting the GOP have sought to flip the script, accusing Democrats of taking money from donors who had ties to Epstein. During a Georgia Senate debate, Collins accused his opponent, Jon Ossoff, of accepting campaign donations from Reid Hoffman, a tech billionaire who had ties to Epstein. Hoffman has said he only knew Epstein through fundraising relationships and regrets it. “You can claim to fight against the Epstein class, but I’m going to tell you, this call is coming from inside the house and the Epstein class is on stage right now and it’s you,” Collins said . In New Mexico’s gubernatorial race, an outside group released an ad accusing Democratic candidate Deb Haaland of accepting a ride on Epstein’s private jet and taking “tens of thousands of dollars from Epstein businesses” and then “asking for more”. Haaland did not fly on Epstein’s jet, but did take a flight booked by one of Epstein’s companies in 2014. Haaland has said she was unaware the chartered flight was owned by an Epstein-owned company. https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/10/mwc2.text: The Middle East and North Africa’s mobile economy is projected to reach €421 billion by 2030, but a new industry report highlights a persistent problem: economic growth is accelerating, yet millions of people still are not benefiting from the digital economy.GSMA’s Mobile Economy MENA 2026 report, released on the opening day of MWC26 Doha, revealed that mobile technologies and services generated an estimated €340 billion in economic value in 2025, supporting 2.2 million jobs and contributing around €35.8 billion to public finances.Meanwhile, 48% of MENA’s population used mobile internet last year, while 49% remained offline despite living in areas covered by mobile networks.The figures point to a challenge that extends beyond infrastructure: ensuring people can afford, access and use the technology available to them.Doha at the centre of the global connectivity debateThis year’s MWC26 Doha carries added significance as it takes place alongside the International Telecommunication Union’s Plenipotentiary Conference, the first time the two events are being held at the same location.The two gatherings bring industry leaders and policymakers together at a time when decisions on connectivity standards, digital infrastructure and technological governance will help shape how the global digital economy evolves.Held in partnership with Qatar’s Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, the three-day MWC26 Doha aims to advance digital connectivity while also creating meaningful access for consumers.The event is also being held as the region faces continued uncertainty over the future of the US-Iran war, but opening-day turnout has signalled resilience in the ICT industry and that connectivity remains a business priority.Building the infrastructure behind the AI boomAs AI systems rapidly evolve to carry out more complex tasks autonomously, the industry faces growing pressure to provide the computing power, capacity and resilience needed to support them.Speaking at the opening ceremony on Sunday, Qatar’s Minister of Communications and Information Technology, Mohammed bin Ali Mannai, noted the rise of AI agents was increasing the need for more resilient networks and advanced computing capabilities. For GSMA Director General Vivek Badrinath, the region’s digital future depends not only on expanding connectivity, but also on ensuring networks, services and devices work across borders and communities.“Progress only counts if everyone shares in it. That means two things: global standards that keep networks, services and devices working across borders, and a concerted effort to connect the people who are still offline,” Badrinath said at the opening ceremony.Speaking to Euronews, he acknowledged that the industry had not done well in the past year to make mobile connectivity more affordable to the people who really need it.“A year ago, we were hoping to be able to bring to the market smartphones in the $50 range. That's very much impossible today with the increase of RAM prices driven by the huge demand for AI. This is an unfortunate side effect,” Badrinath said.He added that strong demand for AI is depriving smartphone producers of the resources they need to make entry-level phones. Still, investment forecasts are encouraging. GSMA projects that operators will invest around €80 billion across MENA between 2025 and 2030. But the challenge is ensuring these investments translate into services people and businesses can use. Quantitative models: AI’s next frontierWhile connectivity has become the foundation of most AI functions, the technology is moving fast beyond content generation and chatbots, expanding into fields such as scientific research, healthcare, materials, and energy.In an interview with Euronews, SandboxAQ CEO Jack Hidary said quantitative AI approaches can help tackle complex problems traditional methods may still struggle to solve.“The second bucket of AI is AI for the physical world, for the real world. We look at biomedicine, energy, financial services, these big sectors are really areas for LQM and LLMs, so it's great to see the convergence of these two now,” Hidary said.Fresh from a recent deal with Anthropic and a €449 million R&D award from the US Commerce Department, Hidary believes these milestones will give the company leverage to innovate further.“It's a very exciting new award that we got to focus on batteries, on magnets, on the things that we need to produce semiconductors in the United States so that we can really power the economy,” he added.Narrowing the digital divideExtending network coverage alone will not be enough to prevent the onset of a second digital divide if governments and policymakers do not commit to removing barriers like smartphone affordability, access to data packages, and the skills needed to use digital services. These barriers risk becoming more consequential as AI reshapes industries and workplaces, impacting people without the tools or training.Assistant Resident Representative and Inclusive Growth and Innovation Team Leader at UNDP Egypt Abeer Shakweer echoed GSMA’s call for growth that benefits all segments of society. “Globally, women, persons with disabilities, people in remote and rural areas, and vulnerable young people are at most at risk of being left behind,” she told Euronews in an interview.Through acceleration programmes that expand access to financial services and new markets, as well as supporting youth at the ideation stage, Shakweer's work at UNDP Egypt helps empower young entrepreneurs and innovators as real contributors to growth.Ultimately, rapid advancements in the digital economy should not only be about the technology deployed, but about how it gives people the opportunity to shape it, contribute to it, and benefit from it.Turning connectivity into everyday valueOne way connectivity has opened up a tangible pathway for inclusive growth is through financial services.Mobile wallets and digital payments platforms can give people and businesses new ways to send and receive money, giving merchants a chance to reach more customers and manage transactions more easily.Mirko Giacco, CEO of Ooredoo Fintech, works at the intersection of connectivity and financial services, tapping into the parent company's vast network while also prioritising underserved communities in the MENA region, such as Tunisia, Oman, the Maldives and Qatar.“In Qatar, more than 20% of the market share international remittance goes through our products. That means we give users, migrant workers that are here, the tools to send money back home. They do it with us in a way that is safe, convenient, and economically viable,” Giacco told Euronews.Meanwhile in the Maldives, Ooredoo Fintech has been the first fintech company to enable gig workers to receive payments in US dollars, through a partnership with PayPal. The GSMA also released a report at MWC26 Doha which looks at how operators in MENA are turning network investments into sustainable returns. The 5G Monetisation MENA report found that 17 of the region’s 24 markets had launched commercial 5G services by September 2026, while 5G connections are expected to rise from 67 million in 2025 to almost 350 million by 2030.
